title: The House That Counted
summary: Mira's aunt lives in a house with one rule: never count the rooms. On a bored afternoon, Mira counts — and the house, proud to have finally been noticed, begins to grow to deserve the attention.

chapters.title: Never Count the Doors
chapters.body:
Aunt Odilia's house stood at the end of a street that climbed, and then climbed a little more, as if it didn't want to arrive. It was a tall, narrow house, the color of old mustard, with windows of sizes that didn't match — some wide, some thin as slits, one round up high like an eye.

Mira was going to spend two weeks there while her parents traveled, and the first thing Aunt Odilia said, before even "hello," before even taking her bag, was:

"One rule, my dear. In this house, we never count the rooms. Never. Not out loud, and not in your head." She smiled, but the smile held a second longer than any smile should. "Promise?"

"I promise," said Mira, the way you promise things you think are silly: quickly, to be done with the matter.

Aunt Odilia was a kind and odd woman, the sort who talk to their plants and leave saucers of milk on the porch "for whoever needs it." Her house was full of clocks that told different times and hallways that took turns before arriving where they should. There was always a good smell of bread and cinnamon, and there was always, underneath, an attentive silence — as if the walls were listening.

For the first few days, Mira even liked it. Her aunt told stories, taught her to make jam, let her stay up late reading. But two weeks is a long time for a girl of twelve in a house with no other children, no phone that got a signal, nothing to do on the long afternoons when her aunt dozed.

And it was on one of those afternoons, bored to the bone, lying upside down on the sofa watching the world in reverse, that Mira began to notice the doors.

There were many. From the sofa, she could see the living room door, the kitchen door, the one to the hallway, the one to her aunt's room, the closet, the downstairs bathroom. Six, just from there. And the hallway had more. And the upstairs, more still. The house was small from outside — Mira remembered thinking it narrow when she arrived — but inside it seemed to have too many doors to fit.

"What a strange house," she thought. "How many doors does it have?"

And then her aunt's rule came back into her head, and — exactly the way a silly rule does when you're bored — instead of pushing it away, she pulled it closer. Don't count the rooms. What a senseless rule. What was going to happen? Would the house take offense?

Mira got up off the sofa. She looked at the long hallway, with its doors on one side and the other.

"Just to see," she thought. "No one will know."

And she began to count.

chapters.title: The Extra Room
chapters.body:
One, the living room door. Two, the kitchen. Three, the hallway. Mira walked slowly, pointing with her finger, counting under her breath, feeling half silly and half brave. Four, five, six on the ground floor. She went up the stairs — which creaked in a way that sounded, for an instant, like a sigh. Seven, eight, nine, ten upstairs.

At the end of the upstairs hallway was a door Mira didn't remember seeing. Narrow, mustard-colored like the house, with a porcelain handle. Eleven.

She stopped. She frowned. She was sure — almost sure — that this hallway had only bedrooms until last week. That door at the end… was it new? No. Doors don't get born. She just hadn't noticed it before. That was all.

Mira went on, because now she was near the end, and giving up in the middle of a count is the hardest thing there is. She opened door eleven.

It led to a small, empty room, with a single thin window. There was nothing inside, only dust and a grey light. But in the opposite corner there was another door. One that, if the room were the size it seemed, shouldn't fit there — it should open onto the outside of the house, onto the air.

Twelve.

Mira felt a chill at the back of her neck. Something was wrong with the math of that house. She should have stopped. She should have run down and woken her aunt and apologized. But curiosity, once it catches fire, burns good sense first. She crossed the empty room and opened door twelve.

Another hallway. One she had never seen, with the same wallpaper, the same clocks telling wrong times on the walls — but darker, as if the afternoon there were later than in the rest of the house. And doors. Many doors, on one side and the other, vanishing into the dark at the far end.

Thirteen. Fourteen. Fifteen.

Mira stopped again, and this time her heart was pounding. She knew that house. She had lived in it for twelve days. And that hallway did not exist. It couldn't exist. The house was narrow. The house was small.

But the more she counted, the more the house had to count.

That was when she understood — too late, the way we always understand these things — what her aunt's rule had meant. The house was not big. The house grew. And it grew when someone counted it, because counting is a way of paying attention, and that house, old and forgotten at the end of a street that didn't even like to arrive, had an ancient hunger to be noticed. Every number Mira said was like a compliment. And the house, proud, flattered, made one more room to deserve the next number. One more door. One more hallway. Growing into itself like a shell that won't stop coiling.

Mira turned to go back.

The empty room she had come through was no longer behind her. In its place was one more door. And another after it. The way back had become the way forward. Every step she had taken inward, the house had turned into more house.

"Auntie?" Mira called, and her voice came out thin, swallowed by the hallway. "AUNT ODILIA!"

Only the clocks answered, ticking off the hour, and — Mira could have sworn — the walls seemed to nestle a little closer, satisfied, like a cat that has finally been given a lap.

chapters.title: Counting the House Down
chapters.body:
Mira could no longer find the way back, and crying wasn't helping, so she did the only sensible thing a girl lost in a hungry house can do: she sat on the hallway floor, leaned against the wall, and made herself think.

"The house grows when I count," she thought. "Every number makes a room. I got to… fifteen. That's as far as I counted."

And the wall at her back was warm. Alive. Waiting for sixteen. The house wanted her to go on. It wanted more attention, more numbers, more compliments — and as long as Mira gave it what it wanted, the house would grow forever, and Mira would walk inside it forever, always one room behind the exit.

That was when Mira had the idea. If counting up made the house grow… perhaps counting down would make it shrink. If saying the numbers in order was a compliment that made rooms, saying them in reverse might be the opposite of a compliment. A way of taking attention back. Of undoing.

It was only an idea. It could be completely wrong. But it was all she had, and sometimes a fragile idea at the right moment is worth more than a certainty that arrives too late.

Mira stood up. She faced the dark hallway, full of proud doors. And, with the firmest voice she could manage — because the house, she sensed, fed on fear as much as on attention — she began to count down.

"Fifteen," she said, and took a step forward, toward the nearest door.

The wall at her back shuddered. It didn't like that. From the far end of the hallway came a long, wounded creak.

"Fourteen," said Mira, going through the door. On the other side was the empty room again — or one just like it. She didn't stop to make sure. "Thirteen."

And the house began to shrink. Every number she took away, a door closed behind her and did not open again. The dark hallway grew shorter with each step, the walls drawing back with a dry sound of wood, like an old person crossing their arms, offended, turning their face away. The grey light brightened. The clocks, one by one, stopped ticking.

"Twelve. Eleven." Mira walked fast now, almost running, and the house folded up behind her like a closing fan. "Ten. Nine. Eight."

She recognized the upstairs hallway — the real one, the one with the bedrooms. The narrow door with the porcelain handle was there at the end, but shrinking, growing smaller and smaller, as if the house were reabsorbing it, ashamed to have shown it.

"Seven. Six." The stairs. Mira went down them two at a time. "Five. Four."

The ground floor. The living room. The sofa where it had all begun, still bearing the mark of her body.

"Three. Two."

And then she stopped. Because she understood that she couldn't reach zero. Zero rooms would be no house at all, and she was inside the house, and her aunt was asleep somewhere in the house. Counting all the way down would not save her — it would erase her along with it.

Mira stopped at two. She stood in the middle of the living room, out of breath, her heart pounding, and said, aloud, to the walls that were now the right size again, the narrow little house she knew:

"Two. And I stop here. I won't count anymore. Not up, not down." She took a deep breath. "I'm sorry I counted. You don't have to grow for me to notice you. I already noticed. You're a strange house full of wrong clocks and I… I kind of like you. But the way you are. Not bigger."

There was a long silence. And then the house did something Mira didn't expect: the walls warmed again, but in a different way — not hungry. Content. The smell of bread and cinnamon came back, stronger, like a hug. One of the clocks, on its own, began to tick again — slowly, calmly, on the right hour for the first time.

Aunt Odilia appeared in the bedroom doorway, rubbing the sleep from her eyes, her hair mussed.

"Mira? I heard you talking. Is everything all right, dear?"

Mira looked at her aunt. She looked at the house. And she decided that some truths you keep to yourself, so as not to worry those you love.

"Everything's fine, Auntie," she said. "I was just… talking to the house."

Aunt Odilia stopped. She looked at her niece for a long moment, and something in her face — a very old, very tired relief — told Mira that her aunt knew. That she had always known. That perhaps the rule was not superstition, but the one lesson she had to give.

"It answers, doesn't it?" the aunt said quietly. "When you stop demanding and start liking."

Mira nodded.

For the rest of the two weeks, she never counted a single room again. And when she left, bag in hand, standing at the door of that tall, narrow, mustard-colored house, she laid her palm on the entryway wall — just for a moment — and felt, or imagined she felt, the house nestle gently against her hand, the way a cat does to say, in its proud old way, that it had liked her too.
